title.en: Can a splash of colour be a pattern?

text.en: Fold a sheet of paper, drop some colour in the middle, press and open it. You get a lovely design that looks the same on both sides! In this chapter we play with folding, paper planes, mirrors, letters, numbers and tiles to find out what symmetry is and where it hides around us.

Take a sheet of paper and fold it exactly in half. Then open it and drop a few spots of water colour along the fold. Close the paper, press it gently and open it again. Look at the beautiful design you made. The two halves look like each other, like a face and its reflection. That is why the design is called symmetrical. The fold line that divides the design into two equal halves is called the line of symmetry. You already met it when you made masks and rangolis in Class 3.
Now let us fold a paper aeroplane by following the pictures step by step. Mark the line of symmetry in the middle of the folded plane. Its left half and right half are exact copies. If you place a small mirror on this line, the reflection of the right half looks just like the left half. Fly the plane. It flies straight because both sides are balanced and equal. Try making a plane that is not symmetrical, with one wing bigger or bent. Fly both planes and see which stays in the air longer. You will find that the symmetrical plane usually glides better.
Rani folds a paper twice and cuts a small corner. When she opens it, the cut appears in all four parts of the paper. Every fold makes the cut repeat once more, because each fold doubles the number of parts. So if you fold a paper once and cut a notch on the fold, one cut makes two matching holes after opening. If you fold twice, you get four matching holes. Try this and guess first, then open the paper to check your guess.
A shape is symmetrical if we can fold it along a line so that the two parts fit exactly on each other. That fold line is its line of symmetry. Some shapes have more than one line. A square has four lines of symmetry, two through the middle of opposite sides and two along the diagonals. A rectangle that is not a square has only two lines of symmetry, one up and down and one across. Its diagonals are not lines of symmetry, because folding along one does not make the corners match. An equal-sided triangle has three lines of symmetry, one from each corner to the middle of the opposite side. A shape that cannot be folded into two matching halves has no line of symmetry, and we call it asymmetrical.
A mirror shows the reflection of whatever stands next to it. The line where the mirror stands is called the mirror line or line of reflection. Put a mirror along a line of symmetry and half of the shape looks like the whole shape. Try this with digits. The numbers 0, 1 and 8 look the same in a mirror held beside them, if the mirror stands upright on the right side of the digit. A number like 181 or 686 can look the same in a mirror, because the digits on the left and right match as mirror images. Here is a puzzle: think of a 3-digit number near 120 that looks the same in a mirror. Check numbers like 101 and 111, whose first and last digits are the same, and ask where the mirror should stand. Make your own puzzles for friends like this.
Look at the word AMBULANCE written on the front of an ambulance. The letters are written backwards on purpose. The driver ahead sees it in the rear-view mirror, and in the mirror the letters turn around and read correctly. Letters like A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y look the same in the mirror beside them, but letters like C, D and E need the mirror placed above or below. Write a short word, like CAT or WOW, in mirror style and let friends guess it. You can do this in your own language too.
A tile is a shape that is repeated again and again to cover a floor or wall. When tiles are placed well, there are no gaps and no overlaps. To continue a pattern we first find the repeating unit, the part that is repeated. Changing the position or colour of a tile gives a new look. We can slide, flip or turn a tile. Bablu Chacha makes tiles by joining two or more shapes. You can design some of your own and check which of them are symmetrical.
Take a square paper, cut a small piece from one side and slide it to the other side, then tape it. This makes a new tile. The tile still fits perfectly with other copies of itself, with no gaps and no overlaps. Trace the new tile again and again on a large sheet, add eyes and whiskers, and you will see a wall full of cats. This slide, cut and paste trick makes many creative tiles for floors and walls.
Symmetry is everywhere in nature. A butterfly, a leaf, a petal and a flower often look the same on both sides of a line. Go for a nature walk with your teacher or parents and collect fallen leaves and petals. Sort them into symmetrical and not symmetrical ones, and make greeting cards or animals with them. Not everything in nature is symmetrical, so we check each leaf by folding it.

problem.en: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle (not a square) have?

text.en: A rectangle has two pairs of equal sides.

why.en: Think of folding it along the middle.

text.en: Fold from the middle of the top to the middle of the bottom, and the two halves match. Fold from middle left to middle right, and they also match.

why.en: Both folds make two equal halves.

text.en: The diagonals do not work, because folding along a diagonal does not make the corners fit.

why.en: So a rectangle has only 2 lines of symmetry.

problem.en: Rani folds a paper twice and makes one cut at a corner. How many cuts will appear when she opens it?

text.en: The first fold doubles the paper to 2 layers.
The second fold makes it 4 layers.
One cut goes through all 4 layers, so 4 matching cuts appear when the paper is opened.

why.en: A cut made once repeats in every layer.

prompt.en: Explain what a line of symmetry is and how to find it in a shape.

requiredIdeas.en: A line of symmetry divides a shape into two equal halves
The two halves match exactly when folded or seen in a mirror
Fold the shape or place a mirror and check that the halves match
Some shapes have many lines, some have one, some have none

commonMisconceptions.en: A diagonal of a rectangle is a line of symmetry
Any line through a shape is a line of symmetry
Symmetry only happens in drawings, not in nature

points.en: A line of symmetry splits a shape into two halves that match exactly.
A square has 4 lines, a rectangle 2, an equal-sided triangle 3.
A mirror on the line shows the other half, and mirror writing reads correctly in a mirror.
Tiles fit with no gaps and no overlaps, and nature has many symmetrical things.
Each fold doubles the layers, so a cut repeats after unfolding.
